body: looks like fair critic. Could you open a PR?
I have no idea how to open a pull request in this setup :) I have not implemented the proposed changes, and have no code to merge. Sorry ...

1.  might only be a documentation issue, but I'm not sure. The [example](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/examples/covariance/plot_mahalanobis_distances.py#L108) actually takes the square root.
   The question is whether the [outlier detection](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/master/sklearn/covariance/outlier_detection.py#L65) expects squared or non-squared values. I'm not sure.

@amueller If something is called "Mahalanobis distance", then I would expect it to follow the generally accepted definition, such as http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahalanobis_distance. Then, the examples need not take the np.sqrt anymore. The outlier detection method does not depend on this being changed.

However, I checked the docs of R, and their **mahalanobis** function returns "the squared Mahalanobis distance" https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-patched/library/stats/html/mahalanobis.html. Well, I would then agree if your documentation is adjusted like this. Thanks :)
I just would like to double check that the algorithms that use the function actually want squared mahalanobis distances. Maybe @VirgileFritsch (or anyone else) to confirm.

Strangely enough, in many places Mahalanobis distance is raised to the power of `0.33`, that is, a cubic root is taken.

It looks like this allows us to approximate Mahalanobis distance with normal distribution. The square of Mahalanobis distance [has](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahalanobis_distance#Normal_distributions) Chi-square distribution, which is [approximately](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noncentral_chi-squared_distribution#Approximation) the cube of a Gaussian r.v.

So the code looks correct.

issue.title: EmpiricalCovariance and EllipticEnvelope use unsquared Mahalanobis distance, documentation says squared Mahalanobis distance
issue.body:
EDIT: sorry, I must have been blind, I completely missed that the return value of the `mahalanobis` method is now squared.

I guess the only actionable remaining issue is that the documentation should consistently talk about squared Mahanalobis distance everywhere.

<details>
  <summary>ORIGINAL QUESTION</summary>
  
In 2015, [it was observed](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/4168) that the `mahalanobis` method of `EmpiricalCovariance` (and by extension `EllipticEnvelope`) implements squared Mahalanobis distance, whereas the documentation simply said Mahalanobis distance. Accordingly, the documentation of the method [was changed](https://github.com/rasbt/scikit-learn/commit/08f581c36051afa9755d2a8d2e62698e47102034) (but not other references to the Mahalanobis distance in other methods of EllipticEnvelope, nor [here](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/outlier_detection.html)).

In 2018, the implementation in the `mahalanobis` method [was replaced](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/10686) with a call to `pairwise_distances` in `metrics.pairwise`, which calls scipy. But scipy [calculates](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.spatial.distance.mahalanobis.html) unsquared Mahalanobis distance (by applying a square root to the formula for squared Mahalanobis distance). This effect was probably not intentional, and the documentation was not changed.

I suggest we either:

* change the documentation of the `mahalanobis` method to remove the word squared, and maybe even explicitly state that it is unsquared, or;
* square the return value of `pairwise_distances`, change the method name to `squared_mahalanobis` and insert the word squared everywhere to avoid any possible confusion.

In addition, the `contamination` parameter and the `offset_` attribute may or may not be misconfigured with one choice or the other, and would have to be fixed.

The thing is, like the contributors in the first thread, I'm not sure which choice makes inherently more sense and/or is more conventional. We should probably try to follow the literature, but I haven't been able to find anything very explicit on the matter. It might help to consider the interpretation of the Mahalanobis distance in 1 dimension, where it is supposed to correspond to standard deviations.
</details>
